item.title: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Hemiplegic cerebral palsy results from a unilateral prenatal or perinatal brain injury and causes motor impairments in the contralateral side of the body. Variable functional outcomes among children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy despite similar lesion extent suggest that developmental neuroplasticity and brain reorganization contribute to motor function. By using multimodal neuroimaging, we characterize the structural and functional reorganization of the motor system and examine its associations with lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. We examined 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls using electromagnetic source imaging to map the primary motor cortex and characterize movement-related oscillations across physiologically relevant frequency bands, navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation to assess motor cortical excitability and lateralization, and functionally guided diffusion-weighted MRI to evaluate the structural integrity of descending motor and motor commissural fibers. We further assessed upper-limb function using Melbourne Assessment 2 and examined multimodal relationships using correlation, cross-validated latent-variable, and mediation analyses. Children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy showed microstructural abnormalities in the descending motor and motor commissural fibers, characterized by lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (all P < 0.05). The navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children (77%) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, accompanied by reduced contralesional primary motor cortex lateralization (P < 0.05). The hemiplegic cerebral palsy group also exhibited hemisphere-specific abnormalities in movement-related oscillations, including reduced theta synchronization in the contralesional hemisphere and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization in the ipsilesional hemisphere (all P < 0.05). Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance (Rho = -0.74 to -0.57, P < 0.05). Reduced descending motor fiber integrity was associated with impaired dexterity and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization (Rho = -0.51 to 0.62, P < 0.05), while motor commissural fiber integrity was associated with corticospinal motor lateralization (Rho = -0.45 to 0.41, P < 0.05). A cross-validated multimodal structural-functional model predicted motor function (Q^2 = 0.42, P < 0.001) more accurately than structural measures alone (Q^2 = 0.25). Beta-band desynchronization mediated the association between descending motor fiber integrity and motor performance (indirect effect = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.03-0.24). Developmental motor neuroplasticity in hemiplegic cerebral palsy reflects an integrated structure-physiology-behavior process rather than the direct consequence of lesion burden alone. Multimodal biomarkers may improve prognostication and support individualized rehabilitation and neuromodulation.

item.title: Microstructure predicts cognition following deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.

item.title: Diffusion-based vertex-wise connectomics encodes individual differences in cognition, affect and pathology
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
No two brains are wired alike, and much of a person's cognitive and clinical state is written in this individual variation, not in the group average. Structural connectomes, however, are typically read through group atlases that summarize connectivity into regional averages, leaving this individual signal untapped. We build a vertex-wise structural connectome, in which every cortical surface vertex is a node, and apply it across the Alzheimer's continuum. Using an independent dataset for methodological development and a multisite cohort of 317 participants from ADNI-4, we show that connection distance and organizational scale form a nested hierarchy, from a long-range backbone to fine, short-range structure. The individual fingerprint is strongest in medium- and short-range connections and becomes less distinctive as connectivity is pooled into atlas parcels. This individual structure can be recovered across spatial scales, although its fidelity depends on diffusion acquisition quality, with multishell data providing a more informative reference than single-shell data. In the aging brain, an individually referenced balance between short- and long-range connectivity is associated with episodic memory, cognitive reserve, depressive symptoms, and shared molecular pathology. While cognitive associations largely reflect diagnostic differences, associations with depressive symptoms and pathology burden remain detectable after adjustment for diagnosis. These findings show that individual structural connectomes retain clinically and biologically relevant variation that is not fully captured by diagnostic classification or group-level summaries.

item.title: Genetic, metabolic and hippocampal myelin contributions to episodic memory ageing
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract There is ongoing controversy about the role of the apolipoprotein-E (APOE) genotype in modulating cognitive trajectories in healthy ageing and Alzheimer’s disease. We investigated associations between APOE genotype, cardiometabolic and inflammatory profiles, lifestyle, and hippocampal microstructure with late-life episodic memory trajectories in a community-dwelling, mid-to-old-age cohort. The genotyped sample (n = 5325) with follow-up spanning over 20 years included nested cognitive (n = 1378) and neuroimaging subsamples (n = 301). We first tested whether the APOE ε4 allele was associated with systemic physiological profiles across adulthood, followed by assessment of APOE associations with cognitive ageing trajectories and their relationships with health profiles and MRI markers of hippocampal myelination. APOE ε4 carrier status was associated with an adverse lipid-related metabolic profile across adulthood. In late-life, APOE ε4 was selectively associated with steeper age-related episodic memory decline across cognitive domains examined, with effects emerging in the eighth decade of life and evident already among heterozygous carriers. Individual metabolic, inflammatory, cardiovascular, and lifestyle markers did not account for this APOE ε4-related memory effect. When considered jointly within their respective domains, adverse metabolic burden was associated with poorer episodic memory performance and reduced odds of memory maintenance, whereas a favorable lifestyle profile was associated with better episodic memory function, independently of APOE genotype. The association between hippocampal myelin content and steepness of episodic memory trajectories was stronger in APOE ε4 carriers, while hippocampal volume showed only a trend. These findings indicate that APOE ε4 is primarily linked to episodic memory decline dynamics, with hippocampal myelin marking trajectory differences, whereas peripheral metabolic burden and lifestyle relates to memory performance level.

item.title: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface training for upper-limb rehabilitation after subacute stroke: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
item.description:
PloS one
To determine whether motor imagery (MI) based brain-computer interface (BCI) training improves upper-limb motor function in patients with subacute stroke compared with a high-fidelity sham-BCI control, and to explore accompanying structural and resting-state functional MRI changes. In this participant-blinded randomized controlled trial, 32 patients with subacute stroke were randomized to a MI-based BCI group or a high-fidelity BCI sham-control group (n = 16 each). Both groups received dose-matched training (30 min/session, 5 sessions/week for 4 weeks) in addition to standard rehabilitation. Upper-limb motor outcomes were assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE; primary outcome), Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), Motor Assessment Scale (MAS), and Modified Barthel Index (MBI). Structural MRI and resting-state functional MRI were acquired at baseline and post-intervention to assess gray matter volume (GMV) and functional connectivity (FC). Both groups showed significant improvement after the intervention. Compared with the sham-control group, the MI-based BCI group demonstrated greater gains in FMA-UE and secondary motor outcomes (WMFT and MAS), whereas the difference in MBI was not statistically significant. Voxel-based morphometry revealed a within-group increase in GMV in the contralesional supplementary motor area (SMA) in the MI-based BCI group; however, no significant between-group GMV difference was observed. The MI-based BCI group also exhibited increased resting-state FC between the SMA and the ipsilesional cerebellar lobule IX and fusiform gyrus. Changes in FC were associated with improvements in FMA-UE, WMFT, and MBI, but not MAS. Compared with a high-fidelity sham-control group, MI-based BCI group training was associated with greater upper-limb motor recovery in patients with subacute stroke, accompanied by changes in structural and functional neuroimaging measures involving motor-related regions and connections. Larger randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are required to confirm durability and clinical relevance. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2100052452.

item.title: Balance dısorders and structural and connectıvıty changes in the cerebellum in bıpolar dısorder: A dıffusıon tensor imagıng study.
item.description:
The neuroradiology journal
The aim of this study was to evaluate balance performance in individuals with bipolar disorder (BD) and to examine changes in white matter connections associated with cerebellar structures using cranial magnetic resonance (MR) imaging.The study included 30 BD patients and 25 healthy controls with available cranial MR images. Balance performance was assessed, and tractography analyses examined the pathways of the superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP), middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP), inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP), medial lemniscus (LM), and vermis bilaterally. In addition, volumetric measurements of the cerebellum and its subregions were performed.Balance performance was significantly lower in individuals with BD compared to the control group (p < .05). In tractography analyses, a significant decrease in FA values was observed only in the SCP compared to the control group (p = .029). Volumetric analyses revealed a significant decrease in total cerebellar volume in the BB group (p < .05).These findings suggest that individuals with BB may exhibit impaired balance performance, particularly at the SCP level, along with reduced cerebellar volume and limited microstructural changes. While these results suggest a potential role for the cerebellum in the pathophysiology and balance-related mechanisms of BD, they need to be confirmed with a larger sample and longitudinal studies.

item.title: Longitudinal structural connectivity changes and cognitive trajectories in early multiple sclerosis: An exploratory graph-theory study.
item.description:
The neuroradiology journal
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is characterized by focal and diffuse white matter damage, often disrupting structural connectivity, and contributing to cognitive impairment. This exploratory study investigates early connectivity changes in MS and their relationship with cognition.In this longitudinal study, we recruited 18 early MS patients (31.92 ± 8.09 years, disease duration 0.91 ± 1.81 years, 10 females) and matched healthy controls (31.89 ± 8.15 years, 10 females) and acquired structural and diffusion-weighted MRI data at baseline and 10-month follow-up. Patients were categorized as cognitively preserved/recovered (CPR) or cognitively impaired/worsened (CIW) over time. Using graph-theory analysis, we measured network segregation, integration and centrality, and examined group and longitudinal differences.CPR and CIW patients showed distinct longitudinal connectivity patterns considering all nodes: CIW patients showed longitudinal increased segregation and centrality measures (increased strength, local efficiency and clustering coefficient, and decreased participation coefficient), while CPR patients had a longitudinal decrease in centrality and segregation metrics (decrease in strength, local efficiency and clustering coefficient, and increase in participation coefficient).Cognitive impairment is a predominant feature of MS, and might be closely related to structural connectivity changes, even in early MS. Understanding these early exploratory longitudinal associations between connectivity changes and cognition provides hypotheses for future larger studies on potential prevention of cognitive health in MS.

item.title: Volume of the mammillary bodies and cognitive trajectories in preclinical Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
EBioMedicine
As part of the Papez circuit, the mammillary bodies (MB) play a key role in episodic memory, but their contribution to cognitive changes in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains underexplored. Here, we investigated the associations between MB volume and cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired older individuals, and whether these associations differed by Aβ status. We examined 228 cognitively unimpaired older participants from the Harvard Ageing Brain Study (mean age: 73.5 ± 8.0, 64% female, all CDR = 0) who underwent baseline MRI, 11C-Pittsburgh Compound B (PiB) PET imaging and annual cognitive assessments. MB volume was quantified using the FastSurfer-HypVINN tool, and PiB status was derived from a neocortical aggregate. Cognition was assessed over up to 11 years using the Preclinical Alzheimer's Cognitive Composite 5 (PACC5), as well as a memory and executive function composite. At baseline, PiB+ participants with lower MB volume showed poorer cognitive performance on the PACC5 and on memory and executive function composites. Longitudinally, lower baseline MB volume was associated with steeper memory and PACC5 decline, particularly among PiB+ participants. Control analyses showed that associations between posterior hypothalamic volume and cognitive performance, at baseline and over time, did not differ by PiB status. Similarly, associations between hippocampal volume and baseline cognition did not differ by PiB status, but hippocampal volume was associated with cognitive decline, more strongly in PiB+ individuals. These findings indicate that lower MB volume was associated with poorer cognitive performance and steeper decline in PiB+ individuals, suggesting that MB volume may serve as an indicator of cognitive decline in preclinical AD. National Institutes of Health, Alzheimer's Association.

item.title: Postoperative delirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing: an exploratory cohort study.
item.description:
British journal of anaesthesia
Advanced age is a major risk factor for both delirium and dementia. A potential early biomarker for dementia is the brain-predicted age difference (brainPAD). We hypothesised that brain ageing accelerates after postoperative delirium (POD), and that increased brainPAD is associated with cognitive decline. Brain MRI scans were obtained in 287 older patients before and 3 months after major elective surgery, and two MRI scans at similar time intervals were obtained in 46 nonsurgical control participants. We computed grey matter brainPAD in patients with POD (POD+), patients without POD (POD-), and nonsurgical controls. The Trail Making Test (TMT) was administered at both time points to examine associations between changes in brainPAD and changes in attention/processing speed (TMT-A) and executive task switching (TMT-B and TMT B-A). Compared with the POD- group, brainPAD increased by an additional 6 (sd=3) months over time in the POD+ group (P=0.002). For each 1 year-over-year increase in brain age gap, patients took 2.3 s longer to complete the TMT-A (P=0.016), whereas no association was observed with TMT-B (P=0.254) or TMT B-A (P=0.91). Postoperativ edelirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing, which in turn is associated with decline in attention and processing speed. These findings help to understand the complex relationship between ageing, delirium, and dementia. NCT02265263.

item.title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.

item.title: Is Latin American brain anatomy "normal"? Construction and evaluation of a Chilean brain template
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Many neuroimaging processes use a brain reference anatomical template; the most widely used is the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template. Yet studies have shown that different populations exhibit different global brain features, and the use of a unique Canadian template may introduce biases in analyses for other populations. The purpose of this work is to construct a brain template that accurately represents our local population in Chile. In addition, our project explicitly addresses another pressing challenge: the limited availability of high-field MR scanners in Latin America. In this context, we will build our template using a 0.55T MR scanner, thus ensuring not only population specificity but also methodological alignment with the technological realities of our healthcare systems. Healthy volunteers (n = 76, ages 18–60) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Images were preprocessed and iteratively registered via rigid and non-linear steps to generate a Chilean template (CL76). Evaluation involved dimensional comparisons with Canadian, Indian, Chinese, and Korean templates. Deformation metrics were estimated for an additional 23 volunteers. The Chilean template measures 166 × 132 × 100 mm3, smaller than the Canadian one (179 × 137 × 118 mm3), and has distinct proportions, particularly the width/height ratio of 1.31 versus 1.16. Deformation of a test population onto CL76 was significantly lower (p = 0.010) and less variable than that of MNI152. The top deformed regions onto CL76 or onto MNI152 differed, confirming population specificity on the template. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first brain template generated in South America; however, we do not claim to represent the entire continent—only a specific population from Chile. This work highlights the need for broader representation across diverse populations, particularly to counterbalance the current over-representation of individuals from high-income countries with established research and imaging infrastructures.

item.title: Data-Driven Decomposition of Precisely Aligned Fiber-Orientation-Preserving Probabilistic Tractography Connectomes with Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The major goals of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were to characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the human brain. Although there has been tremendous work done for functional connectivity, including application of a variety of data driven decomposition approaches, structural connectivity from the HCP has seen less attention. This work presents a collection of methodological advances that, in combination, enable similar approaches to be applied to diffusion tractography data. Here, we use multi-modal non-linear volumetric alignment with FSL's MultiMOdal Registration Framework (MMORF) to precisely align white matter tracts and globular gray matter nuclei, use the White matter Hierarchical Modelling (WHIM) method to align voxel-wise fiber orientations, enable efficient GPU-accelerated computation and storage of full resolution probabilistic gray matter x white matter x fiber sparse tractography matrices in precise alignment across individuals using the aforementioned MMORF and WHIM alignments together with areal-feature-based cortical surface registration. These tractography dense connectomes can be averaged across individuals and sparse, computationally efficient non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) can be applied to perform data-driven decompositions into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories. The primary outputs of this effort to date are 1) A set of HCP software pipelines enabling such analyses, 2) A new unbiased HCP-derived volumetric standard space that is representative of the young adult brain and follows ACPC orientation conventions across individuals. 3) Reproducible NMF decompositions of HCP young adult tractography data into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories, which could be projected using non-negative dual regression back to individuals. These data represent a starting point for a new generation of data-driven atlasing efforts for human white matter, and these methods can be applied to study the white matter in development, aging, and brain diseases.

item.title: Cerebellum–white-matter proportionality is associated with cognition but not explained by lobular anatomy
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background. A previously identified association between whole-cerebellum and cerebral-white-matter (Cer:WM) allocation and cognitive ability does not establish a lobular mechanism. We tested whether this association in Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) ID1000 was robust to a new cerebellar measurement and explained by regional allocation. Methods. First-run T1-weighted scans from 928 participants were processed outcome-blind with FastSurfer/CerebNet v2.6.0. Before regional measurements were joined to cognition, the primary exposure was fixed as the log ratio of bilateral Crus I, Crus II and VIIb to bilateral lobules I-IV and V. Blinded quality control produced one anatomical exclusion; final analyses used 925 participants and adjusted for age, sex, tissue scale and five-part macroanatomical composition. Results. The newly measured Cer:WM association remained positive (standardized β = 0.101, 95% CI 0.029–0.174, p=.0063; old/new cerebellar totals r=.982). The locked posterior:anterior ratio was null (β = 0.004, 95% CI -0.059-0.067, p=.908); its confidence interval excluded standardized effects of magnitude ≥ 0.067, and a post-hoc equivalence test supported equivalence within ± 0.10 (TOST p=.0014). The regional term attenuated the baseline macro Cer:WM coefficient by only 0.28%. Global lobular-composition and asymmetry tests were null, and regional augmentation was uninformative in cross-validation. Conclusions. The AOMIC Cer:WM association is robust to cerebellar measurement method but is not explained by detectable lobular allocation in healthy young adults. Cerebral white matter and cerebellum showed markedly different intracranial-volume scaling (exponents 0.606 versus 0.372), underscoring allometric and compositional specification as an important benchmark for cerebellar morphometry.

item.title: Diffusion tractography of the olfactory pathway and odor recognition
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Olfactory processing constitutes a unique system where sensory input is directly linked to integrative perceptual processing, providing an optimal model for investigating how perceptual input is transformed into higher-order functions. However, the neural substrates of olfaction remain incompletely understood. Here, we delineated central olfactory pathways using advanced tractography and examined associations between tractography metrics and olfactory functions. We acquired T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted images from 129 healthy participants and assessed olfactory function in 59 individuals using a T&T olfactometer. We defined the primary olfactory cortex and secondary olfactory structures and their connections. White matter query language was used to extract central olfactory pathways from refined whole-brain tractography according to neuroanatomical rules. We analyzed the number of streamlines and the laterality index of these pathways in relation to olfactory detection and recognition thresholds. For the total olfactory fascicle, more streamlines were observed in the left than the right hemisphere, and greater leftward lateralization was significantly associated with lower mean recognition thresholds. In conclusion, we successfully reconstructed central olfactory pathways beyond the primary olfactory cortex and provided evidence supporting the neural basis of higher-order olfactory functions. Leftward lateralization may enhance associative olfactory processing by reducing circuit redundancy and allocating additional neural capacity.

item.title: Correspondence Between Structural and Functional Connectivity Within White Matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract White matter functional networks (WMFNs) derived from resting-state BOLD fluctuations have been identified across multiple datasets, but whether they correspond to coherent anatomical units defined by the underlying axonal architecture remains untested. Here we tested WM structural connectivity-functional connectivity (SC-FC) coupling directly by asking whether regions co-assigned to the same WMFN are preferentially linked by WM tracts. Using resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI from the Human Connectome Project 7T dataset (N = 161), we derived 11 WMFNs per session (after exclusion of one boundary network) via k-means clustering of voxel-level functional connectivity (FC), constructed structural connectivity (SC) using multi-shell multi-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution with anatomically constrained tractography, and quantified the correlation between SC and FC across within- and between-network edges. Within-network coupling was two to three times higher than between-network coupling in both sessions (Session 1: r within = 0.59 vs. r between = 0.20; Session 2: r within = 0.66 vs. r between = 0.28; p < 0.001). The increased coupling was also observed across subjects, in terms of survived matching of edge counts, and disappeared when network labels were permuted. Network-level coupling was heterogeneous and concentrated in projection pathways spanning the midbrain and medulla oblongata, with rank ordering of the six highest-coupling networks identical across sessions. These findings provide structural support that WMFNs are coherent anatomical-functional units and support reconceptualising WM as a structured contributor to the brain's functional architecture rather than a passive transmission medium.

item.title: Quantity and quality of children's screen use and their neural and associated behavioral outcomes: A systematic review.
item.description:
Child development
The developmental impact of screen use on young children remains an active area of inquiry, with evidence of both risks and benefits depending on quantity and quality of exposure. This systematic review synthesized 23 neuroimaging studies of children aged 0-8 years, selected from 19,699 records identified across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and APA PsycINFO (2012-2025). Studies were included if they examined typically developing children, employed neuroimaging methods (EEG, fNIRS, or MRI), and assessed the effects of digital media exposure or intervention on brain and associated outcomes. Eight studies on quantity associated greater screen exposure with lower prefrontal activation, altered cortical activity, differences in white matter pathways, and lower myelination in language and cognitive regions. Fifteen studies on quality found that interactive and multimodal media, educational gamification, and caregiver co-use enhanced networks supporting language, perception, and socioemotional skills, whereas non-educational media showed null effects. Our paper argues that discussions on screen use should move beyond the sole focus on duration of screen-time to consider the dimensions of design, content, and context of media use and how they may shape developmental outcomes.

item.title: A reproducible structural brain axis of alcohol use severity.
item.description:
Translational psychiatry
Alcohol use is linked to distributed structural brain alterations, but population-level alcohol-related neurobiology remains difficult to quantify. We tested whether deep learning-derived MRI representations capture reproducible variation in alcohol consumption severity and converge with clinical and biological markers. Representations were extracted from gray-matter volume maps in the German National Cohort (NAKO; N ≈ 28,000). Ridge-regression scores were derived from structural MRI to estimate alcohol consumption severity, measured with the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Consumption (AUDIT-C). Models were trained in NAKO, externally validated in UK Biobank (N ≈ 25,000), evaluated in FOR2107 (N ≈ 1900), and tested against ICD-10 alcohol use disorder (AUD), alcohol-related biomarkers, and cognition. In NAKO, the structural MRI-derived ridge-regression score correlated with measured AUDIT-C severity (r = 0.11; 95% CI, 0.09-0.12; qFDR = 1.2 × 10-70 ; MAE = 1.64). This association replicated in UK Biobank (r = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.07-0.10; qFDR = 4.9 × 10-41 ; MAE = 1.96) and generalized to AUD, with higher odds in the highest versus lowest brain-score quintile (OR = 2.28; 95% CI, 1.49-3.48; qFDR = 3.9 × 10-4 ). The score was associated with gamma-glutamyl transferase (β = 1.17 U/L; qFDR = 0.007), mean corpuscular volume (β = 14.26 fL; qFDR = 4.4 × 10-4 ), and slower reaction time (β = 163.40 ms; qFDR = 3.0 × 10-5 ). Deep learning-derived structural MRI representations capture weak but reproducible alcohol-related brain variation that converges with AUD diagnosis, peripheral biomarkers, and cognition, supporting their use in population-level addiction neuroscience while underscoring limits for individual-level prediction.

item.title: Right-to-left shunt burden and altered white matter functional networks in stroke-free patients with patent foramen ovale.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) is a useful technique for investigating the functional organization of human brain networks. Nevertheless, most rsfMRI studies in patent foramen ovale (PFO) have focused on gray-matter connectivity or structural imaging, whereas white-matter functional networks remain poorly characterized. PFO has been hypothesized to expose the brain to recurrent right-to-left shunt (RLS)-related microembolic, vasoactive and hemodynamic stressors, but whether these stressors are associated with altered white-matter functional organization in patients without overt stroke is unclear. The current study used rsfMRI to evaluate white-matter functional networks in stroke-free PFO patients and healthy controls. In the PFO group, RLS severity and anatomical features were characterized using contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler and transesophageal echocardiography. Nine large-scale white-matter networks were identified by K-means clustering of voxel-wise white-matter functional connectivity. Evaluation of spontaneous oscillations and inter-network functional connectivity showed that PFO patients had widespread reductions in fast Fourier transform-derived band-averaged amplitude, mainly involving motor, occipital, cerebellar, deep and cingulum networks, and consistently reduced inferior frontal-to-fronto-temporal connectivity across frequency bands. Higher RLS grade was associated with lower white-matter amplitude in several networks, whereas PFO anatomical measurements showed no independent associations after multiple-comparison correction. Exploratory mediation analyses showed no significant indirect pathways after FDR correction. In this cross-sectional study, these findings suggest that RLS burden may be relevant to subclinical white-matter functional vulnerability in stroke-free PFO.

item.title: Microstructural disruption of the forceps minor in schizophrenia: a potential clinical imaging biomarker using translational DTI.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Schizophrenia is one of the most complex brain disorders, arising from multidimensional pathophysiological processes that span genetic vulnerability, neurotransmitter dysregulation, structural brain damage, and large-scale brain network dysfunction. Large-scale neuroimaging studies have consistently demonstrated the critical role of frontal brain regions in schizophrenia. Despite substantial progress, the precise localization of structural damage within these regions and the neurobiological mechanisms linking such alterations to disease pathology remain poorly understood. In this study, we included a total of 115 subjects from two sites of the B-SNIP dataset, comprising 60 healthy controls and 55 individuals with schizophrenia. We employed diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to precisely characterize specific structural alterations in the frontal brain regions associated with schizophrenia. Our findings reveal significant microstructural abnormalities in the forceps minor, a major commissural white-matter tract that serves as a critical interhemispheric bridge between the bilateral frontal lobes. Network-level mapping further demonstrates that the forceps minor is closely integrated with large-scale brain networks, particularly the default mode network, and maintains strong structural connectivity with orbitofrontal regions-both of which are known to exhibit dysfunction in schizophrenia. Moreover, converging evidence suggests that the forceps minor plays an important role in the regulation of social behavior, a core domain of impairment in schizophrenia. Collectively, these findings identify the forceps minor as a promising structural imaging biomarker for schizophrenia and provide novel insights into the microstructural mechanisms underlying the disorder.

item.title: Cortical Hypoperfusion in Acute Anorexia Nervosa Is Graded Along the Sensorimotor-Association Hierarchy.
item.description:
The International journal of eating disorders
Objective Cortical gray-matter changes in anorexia nervosa (AN) are among the largest reported in psychiatry, but the functional-metabolic state of that tissue is largely unknown. Because cortical energy use is highest in transmodal association cortex (prefrontal, parietal, and temporal regions of the default-mode and frontoparietal networks), a reduced energy supply predicts a graded rather than uniform reduction in perfusion (blood delivery to tissue). Method A total of 44 acutely underweight women with AN and 45 healthy women underwent 3 T pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling with partial-volume correction. Cerebral blood flow was compared between groups across the Schaefer 100 regions 7 networks atlas, age-adjusted and false-discovery-rate-corrected, and the case-control map was compared with the principal functional gradient (the axis running from sensorimotor to transmodal cortex), with cortical thickness in the same participants, and with 18 PET and SPECT receptor maps. Results Perfusion was lower in AN in 97 of 100 regions and maximal in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex (composite d = -0.56). The deficit scaled with position along the principal functional gradient (ρ = -0.56), an axis unrelated to perfusion in health, and was recoverable in individual brains (d = -0.53). Thinning was widespread but unrelated to gradient position, and the two effect maps did not correspond. Hypoperfusion was greater where D1, CB1, mGluR5, M1, 5-HT2A, and μ-opioid systems are dense, the dopaminergic, cannabinoid, glutamatergic, and muscarinic ones persisting after gradient adjustment. item.title: Beyond morphometry: Adolescent brain microarchitecture reflects sex differences in pubertal timing and hormones
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. Here, we used restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) to link peripubertal hormone levels to individual differences in brain microarchitecture (i.e., cellular and neurite density) in 7,457 youth (ages 9 to 13 years) from the ABCD Study. Sex- and age-stratified multi-task regression analyses identified microarchitecture patterns jointly associated with physical pubertal maturation and each dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), testosterone, estradiol (in female youth), in turn, combining repeated cross-validation with permutation-based feature importance. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.

item.title: Neural correlates of individual differences in cognition: a behavioral performance, EEG, and MRI dataset
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability. The multi-indicator design supports latent-variable modeling of all major constructs alongside their structural, functional, and electrophysiological neural correlates. Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). Electroencephalography (EEG) data was collected during four resting-state blocks and during task performance (cognitive control and processing speed). High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging using the SANDI protocol, and multi-band multi-echo functional MRI during rest and task-switching were acquired in a subset. Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data are accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository. All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.

item.title: Robust sex differences in regional gray matter volume but shared personality-gray matter associations in young adults.
item.description:
PloS one
Relationships between personality traits and brain regions have been widely studied, but potential sex-based differences have received less attention, despite sex hormones affecting neuronal activity and brain functions. We aimed to determine whether the personality-brain relationship differs fundamentally between the sexes. We enrolled healthy university students (103 men, 111 women). Gray matter volumes were measured in 388 brain regions using voxel-based morphometry on T1-weighted brain MRI, and personality traits were assessed using the temperament and character inventory. In confirmatory analyses correcting for multiple comparisons across all 388 regions and seven factors (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate), main-effect sex differences in gray matter volume were robust: 17 regions survived correction, independent of personality, and were predominantly subcortical (thalamus, pallidum and putamen) and right-lateralized. By contrast, neither any association between personality and gray matter volume nor any personality-by-sex interaction survived correction, indicating that personality-gray matter associations were not detectably different between the sexes. In a cross-validated penalized regression over all regions, only self-transcendence was predicted above chance (out-of-sample R2 ≈ 0.04, permutation p = 0.004), and this prediction was essentially unchanged after adjustment for sex and total intracranial volume. In exploratory region-wise analyses (uncorrected p < 0.05), the distribution of brain regions associated with each personality factor appeared to differ between the sexes; for instance, harm avoidance in females was related mainly to parietal, temporal and thalamic regions, whereas in males it was related mainly to sensorimotor and cerebellar regions. These exploratory patterns did not survive correction and are reported as hypothesis-generating observations. Overall, sex differences in this young adult sample were robust for subcortical volume but not for the coupling between personality and gray matter volume, which appeared largely shared between the sexes, underscoring the importance of considering sex as a biological variable while distinguishing confirmed effects from exploratory observations.

item.title: Reverberant magnetic resonance elastography and NODDI provide complementary characterization of age-related brain changes in healthy adults.
item.description:
Physics in medicine and biology
Objective. Age-related changes in brain microstructure and mechanical properties are essential for understanding neurodegeneration and improving early diagnosis. We asked whether tissue microstructure explains the age-related decline in brain stiffness. To test, we related stiffness, measured using reverberant magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), to microstructure, assessed by neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI).Approach. Twenty-eight healthy volunteers (22-76 years) underwent 50 Hz MRE at 3 T. NODDI parameters (isotropic volume fraction Fiso; orientation dispersion index, ODI; neurite density index, NDI) were computed from diffusion-weighted images in 26 subjects. We analyzed global gray and white matter and 13 deep brain regions. Age associations were evaluated using Spearman correlations. Multivariate regression was used to test whether NODDI parameters predicted shear modulus independently of age. All tests used Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction.Main results. Shear modulus decreased with age in both gray matter (,) and white matter (,), and in nine of 13 deep brain regions after FDR correction. Fiso (,) and NDI (,) increased with age in gray matter; no NODDI parameter changed significantly with age in white matter. Across the six global multivariate tests (gray and white matterthree NODDI parameters), only the gray-matter Fiso independently predicted shear modulus after adjusting for age (,); no NODDI parameter predicted white matter stiffness. This association did not survive FDR correction after additional adjustment for sex ().Significance. These findings suggest that cortical free water accumulation is the microstructural measure most closely associated with age-related softening in this cohort, pending confirmation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts, and support a multi-modal approach to characterizing age-related brain changes.

item.title: [Cognitive involvement in adult myotonic dystrophy type 1: new findings from the North].
item.description:
Medecine sciences : M/S
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is the most common adult-onset myopathy, but is also a brain disorder leading to cognitive impairment. This brain condition remains poorly characterized: the scientific literature highlighted different cognitive profiles, and no predominant mechanism has been identified. Recent findings from our team in Lille, France, help to better understand this cognitive impairment. We showed that three distinct cognitive profiles exist, patients probably starting from the least severe to the most severe profile with ageing, while brain abnormalities progress in the anterior regions of the brain (frontal and parietal lobes). Despite this cognitive heterogeneity, some difficulties seemed more frequent in our patients, especially those concerning social cognition (skills especially involved in social interactions), and might be explained by white matter lesions in the temporal poles, but also by neurodevelopmental abnormalities in the right parietal lobe.

item.title: Microstructure regulation of Co3O4via a variable temperature strategy for efficient azo dye degradation by peroxymonosulfate activation.
item.description:
Dalton transactions (Cambridge, England : 2003)
Peroxymonosulfate (PMS)-activated advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) are promising for the removal of refractory azo dyes, and the catalytic performance of Co3 O4 strongly depends on its surface and microstructural characteristics. Herein, Co3 O4 microspheres were prepared by a solvothermal-annealing route, and their microstructures were regulated by varying the annealing temperature from 350 to 650 °C without changing the spinel phase. Increasing the annealing temperature induced progressive nanoparticle coarsening and decreased the BET specific surface area from 7.68 m2 g-1 for Co3 O4 -350 to 1.08 m2 g-1 for Co3 O4 -650. Among the samples, Co3 O4 -350 exhibited the highest PMS activation activity, achieving 99.1% removal of Ponceau Red 2R (PR) within 3 min with an apparent pseudo-first-order rate constant of 1.6693 min-1 . Quantitative comparison with representative Co3 O4 -based PMS activation systems reported in the literature further demonstrates the competitive kinetic performance of Co3 O4 -350, with a catalyst-mass-normalized apparent rate constant of 5.5643 L g-1 min-1 . Radical quenching experiments and EPR measurements support the involvement of SO4 ˙- , ˙OH, O2 ˙- , and 1 O2 in the oxidation process. Co3 O4 -350 also retained 93.7% PR removal after eight consecutive cycles. These results show that simple annealing-temperature regulation can effectively tune the accessible surface structure of compositionally unmodified Co3 O4 and provide a competitive route for PMS activation toward azo-dye degradation.

item.title: The Tapetum: Historical Evolution, Anatomical Insights, and Contemporary Neurosurgical Relevance.
item.description:
World neurosurgery
Objective The tapetum is a thin commissural fiber layer originating predominantly from the splenium of the corpus callosum and forming part of the lateral wall of the atrium and temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. Although surgically relevant, its historical development has received limited attention. This review examines the evolution of the anatomical concept of the tapetum from early descriptions of interhemispheric and ventricular anatomy to contemporary fiber-dissection and tractographic perspectives. Methods A narrative historical review was conducted using classical neuroanatomical texts from the sixteenth to twentieth centuries and contemporary studies identified through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Historical primary sources and modern anatomical, surgical, and imaging studies were reviewed. Results Early concepts of interhemispheric connectivity arose from descriptions of the corpus callosum and ventricular anatomy. Johann Christian Reil formally defined the tapetum in 1809 as a carpet-like layer of callosal fibers lining the lateral ventricular wall. Nineteenth-century anatomists, including Burdach, Arnold, Gratiolet, Flechsig, Meynert, and the Dejerines, refined its topography while highlighting uncertainties regarding adjacent projection and association pathways. Twentieth-century fiber dissection, particularly the Klingler method, enabled three-dimensional visualization, while modern diffusion imaging and tractography supported the interpretation of the tapetum as a thin laminar extension of splenial callosal fibers. Conclusion The tapetum concept evolved from descriptive ventricular anatomy to a fiber-based understanding of posterior interhemispheric connectivity. Its close relationship with the optic radiation and lateral ventricular wall underscores its relevance in contemporary approaches to the atrium and temporal horn.

item.title: Brain volumes and their relationship with cerebral microbleeds and cognition in middle-aged adults with type 1 diabetes.
item.description:
Diabetes research and clinical practice
Aims Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is associated with brain volumetric alterations, cerebral microbleeds (CMBs), and cognitive deficits. We examined brain volumes and their direct and combined associations with CMBs on cognitive performance in T1D. Methods Adults with T1D (n = 163; age 46 ± 8 years; diabetes duration 31 ± 10 years; 53% women) and 48 matched controls underwent brain MRI and clinical and neuropsychological evaluations. Volumetric MRI measures included total brain (TBV) and white matter volume (WMV), and volumes of cortex, thalamus, hippocampus, nucleus accumbens, and choroid plexus. Results Individuals with T1D had smaller TBV, WMV, cortex, thalamus, and nucleus accumbens volumes, and larger choroid plexus, than controls (Cohen's d = 0.39-0.54). Those with T1D and ≥3 CMBs (n = 25) had smaller TBV, WMV, and cortex, thalamus, and nucleus accumbens than those with 0-2 CMBs (n = 138; Cohen's d = 0.54-0.92). Brain volumes were not directly linked to cognition, but CMB burden moderated the associations between TBV, WMV, nucleus accumbens, and choroid plexus and cognitive performance (standardized β: -0.61-(-0.51) and 0.54-0.75, pFDR = 0.006-0.048). Conclusions Middle-aged individuals with T1D showed smaller global and regional brain volumes and larger choroid plexus than healthy controls. Individuals with CMB burden showed associations between brain volumetric alterations and cognitive deficits.

item.title: Transcriptional Patterns of Disruption in Structure-Function Coupling in First-episode, Drug-naive Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience bulletin
First-episode major depressive disorder (FEMDD) is associated with alterations in macroscale brain organization, which may involve changes in brain structure-function coupling (SFC). Whether alterations in SFC affect the emergence of depression and how they correlate with gene expression remain unclear. Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were collected from 95 healthy controls and 124 patients with FEMDD. We applied SFC analysis to calculate the structural decoupling index (SDI) and to quantify SFC in the two groups. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between alterations in SDI and gene expression. The FEMDD group showed a significantly lower SDI in the inferior frontal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, medial orbital gyrus, pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, and lateral occipital cortex (LOcC), whereas a significantly higher SDI was observed in the inferior temporal gyrus, lateral superior frontal gyrus, medial precuneus, and hypergranular insula than in the healthy control group. The speed of processing and working memory scores of the Measurement and Treatment Research to Improve Cognition in Schizophrenia (MATRICS) Consensus Cognitive Battery negatively correlated with the LOcC SDI in the FEMDD group. Additionally, changes in FEMDD-related SDI were associated with the expression of genes involved in synaptic signaling and neuronal development. These findings reveal regional- and network-level alterations in structure-function coupling in patients with FEMDD, providing new insights into the neurobiological underpinnings and promising neuroimaging markers for the prediction of FEMDD.

item.title: Reduced Resting Brain Entropy and Structural-Functional Reorganization in Hearing Loss
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Hearing loss changes how the brain processes sound, yet how chronic auditory degradation shapes the temporal organization of spontaneous cortical activity remains unclear. We examined this question using multimodal MRI from 52 adults with age-related hearing loss and 30 normal-hearing controls. Guided by convergent neuroimaging evidence, we focused on the superior temporal gyrus (STG) and assessed brain entropy (BEN), complementary resting-state measures, and gray matter volume (GMV). Hearing loss was associated with lower BEN in a focal right-STG cluster after adjustment for local GMV (14 voxels; cluster FWER p = 0.008), consistent with more recurrent BOLD signal patterns. Six complementary measures of signal amplitude, local synchrony, symbolic sequence diversity, successive variation, and temporal persistence showed no corrected STG differences. A separate whole-brain analysis revealed higher bilateral midcingulate cortex (MCC) GMV (FWE p = 0.002 and 0.015), motivating examination of the auditory-cingulate relationship. The BEN-defined STG region showed stronger focal functional connectivity with MCC (FWE p = 0.031). Exploratory analyses suggested weaker directed STG-to-MCC influence alongside a small tractography-derived group difference. Exploratory directional comparisons indicated stronger right-MCC GMV-BEN coupling (p = 0.034) and STG-MCC SC-FC coupling (p = 0.037) in controls than in hearing loss. Together, these findings link greater temporal regularity in auditory association cortex to altered auditory-cingulate coordination and local structure-function correspondence, suggesting that adaptation to hearing loss involves both the organization of spontaneous cortical dynamics and their relationship to brain structure.

item.title: ACC Sulcal Morphology as a Neurodevelopmental Marker of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Control among Adolescents
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. BI has been linked to variation in cognitive control, particularly proactive control, a crucial component of executive functions which involves monitoring one's own behavior and adapting that behavior to achieve a particular goal, which may help explain BI's association with elevated anxiety risk. Yet little is known about the neurobiology of cognitive control development among children with BI. Variation in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sulcal pattern asymmetry, established prenatally and stable across development, is associated with individual differences in cognitive control. This preliminary study examined whether ACC sulcal symmetry is associated with BI, proactive and reactive control (measured via the AX-CPT) in adolescents. Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired from 62 adolescents aged 12 to 15 years. ACC patterns in each hemisphere were classified as 'single type' or 'double parallel type' based on the presence of a paracingulate sulcus. Adolescents with symmetric ACC patterns showed lower proactive control ( d ′ context; η 2 p = .091) and greater reactive control (BX probe interference effect; η 2 p = .119). These associations held even when tested within the same statistical model and were comparable in magnitude. ACC symmetry was not associated with BI, nor did it interact with BI to predict cognitive control scores. Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence that ACC sulcal morphology may be a structural marker of variability in cognitive control, with relevance to BI-related neurocognitive risk.

item.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. Methods We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson’s disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. Results Combined saccade–vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade-assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7–49.3%; p≈0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. Conclusions These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. Significance Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

item.title: MR-based normative volumetric analyses reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR -related craniosynostoses
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR -related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non- FGFR -related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non-syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1-weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power-law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR -related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal–frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non-syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

item.title: Bridging brain structure and function: Structural-functional brain network coupling and frontal midline theta connectivity in general intelligence
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC), as well as their alignment (SC-FC coupling), may underlie individual differences in general intelligence. We hypothesized that intelligence emerges from optimized SC-FC coupling and additional processes, namely the task-dependent rapid regulation of FC. To test this hypothesis, we examined MRI-derived SC-FC coupling and EEG-derived midfrontal theta FC dynamics as complementary predictors of intelligence within a latent variable framework. We used a sample of 215 healthy adults (113 females) aged 18–40 years who underwent extensive cognitive ability testing and completed a conceptually similar cued task-switching task during EEG and functional MRI acquisition. Although we found no evidence for a broad association between whole-brain SC-FC coupling and intelligence, an exploratory analysis contrasting functional contexts revealed one for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling computed from task-evoked FC. Specifically, higher coupling predicted higher general intelligence, β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.09, 0.47]. Regarding midfrontal theta connectivity, we found no evidence for an association with intelligence at a preregistered electrode (Fz). However, an exploratory analysis of a broader electrode cluster revealed a temporally specific effect, β = 0.36, 95% CI [0.05, 0.67], suggesting that intelligence may rely on flexible modulation of FC across successive stages of information processing. In a combined model, the two connectivity-based predictors showed no substantial correlation with each other, r = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.25], but both remained significant predictors of intelligence, β = 0.26, 95% CI [0.07, 0.45] for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling and β = 0.22, 95% CI [0.06, 0.39] for late midfrontal theta connectivity. Together, both predictors explained 12.7% of variance in intelligence differences. These findings highlight that the connectivity–intelligence association may be spatially and temporally specific, while emphasizing that intelligence relies on multiple connectivity mechanisms spanning the brain’s structure and function.

item.title: Cortical epigenetic remodeling in transgender men: A first longitudinal study of testosterone treatment.
item.description:
Psychoneuroendocrinology
Previous studies have reported changes in cortical thickness (CTh) following the initiation of gender-affirming testosterone treatment (GATT) in transgender men (TM). However, the precise neurobiological mechanisms and their link to epigenetic factors underlying structural effects remain largely unknown. This longitudinal study, for the first time, characterized testosterone-induced cortical remodeling and explored its association with dynamic DNA methylation (DNAm) in TM after GATT. Forty-three cisgender participants (18 men and 25 women) and 20 TM were included in a longitudinal structural MRI study. Transgender participants were scanned before and after a minimum of five months of GATT. Cortical thickness was quantified using FreeSurfer's longitudinal processing stream. In a subset of 14 TM, genome-wide DNAm was analyzed from peripheral blood using the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip (850 K). Correlations among regional CTh, DNAm profiles, and circulating hormone levels were examined to identify potential molecular-structural associations linked to testosterone exposure. Post-treatment DNAm exhibited a limited set of differentially methylated sites. Exploratory functional annotation of the 27 CpG sites associated with CTh change suggested involvement in biological processes related to transcriptional regulation, protein synthesis, neural signalling, and cellular maintenance. A distinct pattern of longitudinal DNAm changes was observed following testosterone initiation. Several of the affected genes were associated with cortical regions previously implicated in somatosensory and body representation processes. These findings provide preliminary evidence for a relationship between testosterone-related epigenetic remodeling and region-specific variations in CTh. Future studies should examine whether the observed associations are directly linked to body self-perception processes.

item.title: The level of cortical thickening in executive functions and audiovisual integration regions predicts reading comprehension via reading fluency in musically experienced children.
item.description:
Brain research
Proficient reading fluency, which is critical for intact reading comprehension, is related to efficient audio-visual integration and to executive functions (EF). Interestingly, musical training has been associated with better audio-visual integration, EF, and reading abilities. However, the direct relationship, cognitively and neurobiologically, between these components remains ambiguous. Here, we examined the neurobiological correlates of the predictive role of EF and audio-visual integration on reading comprehension through fluency in children with and without music experience using cortical thickness (CT) measures. A high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical scan was acquired from 8- to 12-year-old children with and without music experience. CT within EF (anterior cingulate cortex) and audio-visual (insula) brain regions was compared between groups. A moderated mediation analysis was conducted with anterior cingulate cortex CT as the predictor variable, reading comprehension as the outcome variable, reading fluency as the mediator, and music experience as the moderator, with age and sex as covariates. Musically inexperienced children demonstrated lower reading fluency, comprehension, and EF abilities compared to experienced children. In experienced children, CT in the anterior cingulate gyrus predicted comprehension via an indirect pathway mediated by fluency (B = 21.63, BootSE = 9.11, 95 % CI [4.56, 40.85]); in inexperienced children, neither the direct nor indirect pathways significantly predicted comprehension (B = 11.53, BootSE = 8.64, 95 % CI [-6.54, 28.80]). The Index of Moderated Mediation was not significant (IMM = - 10.10, BootSE = 11.79, 95 % CI [-34.92, 12.21]); thus, there was no statistical evidence that the indirect effect differed between the groups. Results suggest that musical experience is associated with differences in neural circuits linked to EF and audiovisual integration, which in turn relate to reading fluency and comprehension.

item.title: A multi-subject tractography atlas of human cerebellar connections.
item.description:
